stakeholders.name: platform_operators
stakeholders.situation: Design the app-mediated work relationship to satisfy the formal legal tests for independent contracting — no fixed schedule, no direct supervisory title, nominal ability to decline tasks — while retaining algorithmic control over pricing, routing, ratings, and deactivation. Lobbies legislatures and litigates aggressively to keep the formal contract/supervision test as the legal standard, because that test is what keeps the workforce outside statutory employment protections. Captures the difference between labor cost under employment law and labor cost under contractor status directly as margin and shareholder value.

stakeholders.name: platform_investors
stakeholders.situation: Price platform equity partly on the assumption that labor costs remain uncoupled from payroll tax, minimum wage floors, unemployment insurance contributions, and workers' compensation premiums. Have no direct interaction with workers; benefit purely through the valuation effect of the formalist reading holding as the enforced legal standard.

stakeholders.name: platform_workers
stakeholders.situation: Perform the labor that generates platform revenue, subject to algorithmic direction functionally indistinguishable from supervision (route assignment, rating-linked deactivation, dynamic pricing they do not set), but classified outside the legal employment relationship. Bear the full cost of vehicle/equipment depreciation, fuel, unpaid downtime, injury risk, and retirement absence with no employer-side contribution. Exit means leaving the platform entirely for equally precarious alternatives; within the relationship there is no bargaining lever because there is no recognized employer to bargain with.

stakeholders.name: public_insurance_systems
stakeholders.situation: Absorb the safety-net costs — emergency Medicaid, unemployment assistance during downturns, disability support after injury — that an employer would otherwise fund through payroll contributions and insurance premiums under the substantive reading. Cannot decline this cost; it accrues automatically whenever a worker classified as a contractor falls through the gap the formalist boundary creates.

stakeholders.name: traditional_employers_competing_fairly
stakeholders.situation: Operate in adjacent labor markets (taxi companies, delivery firms, staffing agencies) under full employment-law cost structures. Compete against platform operators whose formal classification lets them externalize the same categories of cost. Can lobby for reclassification or exit the labor-intensive segment of their market, but cannot unilaterally adopt the platforms' classification without the same legal exposure the platforms have engineered around.

stakeholders.name: gig_workers_who_value_flexibility
stakeholders.situation: A subset of platform workers — students, caregivers, workers with a second income source — for whom schedule flexibility and low entry barriers are a genuine benefit under contractor status; they would not choose default employment scheduling if offered. Their preference is real but is used rhetorically by platform operators to characterize the entire workforce, most of whom depend on platform income as primary and would prefer employment protections. Largely absent from legislative testimony framed around the median full-time platform worker's situation.

stakeholders.name: labor_regulators_and_courts
stakeholders.situation: Apply and adjudicate the formal contract-and-supervision test case by case. Some regulators actively defer to the formalist reading as settled law; others are actively contesting it through rulemaking (ABC tests, algorithmic-management statutes). Their posture toward the test itself is part of what is contested across the kernel's sibling readings.

six_questions.coordination_function: The contract/supervision test originally solved a real classification problem: distinguishing genuinely independent tradespeople and small businesses (who set their own prices, own their tools, work for multiple clients, bear their own business risk) from employees, so that employer-side obligations attach only where a real subordinate labor relationship exists.
six_questions.transfer_function: Moves the cost of insurance, downtime, equipment, injury risk, and income volatility from the platform operator (who would bear it under employment law) onto the individual worker and, where the worker falls through the resulting gap, onto public insurance systems and general tax revenue.
six_questions.absent_voices: The median full-time platform worker who depends on gig income as a primary source and would prefer employment status is structurally underrepresented in the political and legal narrative, which foregrounds the flexibility-seeking minority; public insurance administrators bearing the externalized cost are rarely named as a party in classification disputes even though they pay directly.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: If the formalist test disappeared and workers were uniformly reclassified as employees, platform unit economics would change substantially: payroll tax, minimum wage floors, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation premiums would attach to the workforce, platform valuations would likely compress, and traditional employers currently competing at a cost disadvantage would see that disadvantage close. Public insurance systems would see reduced downstream claims from uninsured gig injuries and unemployment gaps.
six_questions.founding_problem: Distinguishing genuine independent tradespeople and small contractors — who negotiate their own terms, serve multiple clients, and bear real business risk — from subordinate employees, so that employer obligations track actual control and dependency rather than paperwork alone.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: Platform operators attest the founding problem remains live because their labor model genuinely differs from traditional employment. Labor economists studying algorithmic management (outside the platform industry), several state labor regulators, and the traditional employers bearing the competitive cost attest that the underlying dependency and control the test was built to detect are now present in the platform relationship in substance, and that the formal test has been engineered around rather than genuinely absent — an assessment corroborated by court findings in multiple misclassification rulings against named platform operators.

commentary.narrative_context: This story instantiates the FORMALIST reading of the contested employment boundary kernel: employment status turns on whether a formal contract and direct, named supervisory relationship exist, and platform work — structured to avoid both — sits outside employment law by design. Under this reading, platform workers who value flexibility are not victims of precarity (they chose it), and platforms owe no employer-side obligations because no formal employment relationship was ever created. This is a distinct constraint from the substantive_employment_reading (which locates employee status in economic dependence and algorithmic control regardless of contract form, and would name the full-time gig workforce as victims of misclassification) and from the hybrid_security_reading (which rejects the binary altogether and would not populate a victim/beneficiary set structured around either category). All three share the same underlying kernel — what makes someone an employee — but instantiate structurally different constraints with different ε, different beneficiaries, and different victim sets. Per the ε-invariance principle they are authored as three separate stories linked by network.affects_constraints, not as one story with a measurement parameter.
key_agents: platform_operators: agenda_setter/beneficiary (institutional/arbitrage) — designs classification to sit outside employment law, captures the cost differential
platform_investors: beneficiary (institutional/arbitrage) — benefits from labor-cost externalization reflected in valuation
platform_workers: payer (powerless/constrained) — bears cost of equipment, downtime, injury, and retirement absence under algorithmic direction
public_insurance_systems: payer (institutional/trapped) — absorbs safety-net costs an employer would otherwise fund
traditional_employers_competing_fairly: payer (moderate/constrained) — bears full employment-law costs while competing against externalized-cost platforms
gig_workers_who_value_flexibility: beneficiary/excluded (powerless/mobile) — genuine minority beneficiary whose preference is used to characterize the whole workforce
labor_regulators_and_courts: observer (institutional/analytical) — adjudicates the test case by case, actively contested
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness is authored high (0.78) and rising over the interval because the gap between the cost platforms bear under the formalist reading and the cost they would bear under employment law has widened as algorithmic management tools have grown more precise at exercising de facto supervisory control while avoiding its formal indicators. Suppression is moderate-high (0.62): platform operators actively litigate, lobby, and structure contracts specifically to keep the formalist test as the applicable standard, and workers have no recognized bargaining counterparty within the relationship. Theater ratio (0.40) reflects the growing share of platform operational design (rating systems framed as 'customer feedback' rather than performance management, 'independent scheduling' options that are algorithmically discouraged) that exists specifically to perform the appearance of non-supervision rather than to serve any operational need. Accessibility collapse is moderate (0.50) — genuine independent contracting alternatives exist elsewhere in the economy, but within the platform relationship itself the worker has no path to renegotiate classification. Resistance is substantial (0.68): misclassification lawsuits, state-level ABC test legislation, and worker organizing efforts are active and ongoing, which is itself evidence this is not a settled natural boundary but a contested, actively-defended one.
commentary.directionality_logic: Platform operators and investors sit at the beneficiary end of directionality: the formalist reading is the mechanism by which they avoid employer-side cost, and their exit options (arbitrage — able to relocate, restructure, or exit jurisdictions applying stricter tests) reinforce that position. Platform workers sit at the target end: they bear the substantive costs of a supervised relationship without its formal protections, and their exit options are constrained (leaving one platform means finding another with the same structure, not exiting the classification problem). Public insurance systems and fairly-competing traditional employers are third-party payers who never chose to be parties to the platform relationship but absorb its externalized costs regardless — this is the tangled-rope signature: coordination (matching workers to gig demand) genuinely occurs, but riding on top of it is an asymmetric transfer to non-consenting third parties.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem — distinguishing real independent contractors from subordinate employees — was a legitimate coordination function when it emerged (protecting genuine small-business contractors from being swept into employment mandates they didn't need). Under the formalist reading authored here, that problem is treated as still fully live and correctly solved by the contract/supervision test as applied. The contested status (founding_problem_status: contested) reflects that this is exactly the boundary case mandatrophy analysis exists to catch: a rule built for one population (genuine independent tradespeople) applied to a structurally different population (algorithmically-directed gig workers) without being revisited, while the parties who benefit from the rule's continued application (platform operators) are also the parties most active in defending it as still correctly scoped.
commentary.kernel_context: This constraint instantiates the formalist_employment_reading of the employment_boundary kernel. The kernel is the underlying question 'what makes someone an employee rather than an independent contractor.' Three readings are declared: this one (formal contract + direct supervision as the test), substantive_employment_reading (economic dependence + algorithmic control as the test, which would classify most platform workers as employees and would name them as direct victims of misclassification), and hybrid_security_reading (rejects the binary, proposes a third statutory category with tailored protections). Each reading is authored as its own constraint story with its own ε, beneficiaries, and victims per the ε-invariance principle — this story does not describe or average across the contest, it only instantiates the formalist position and routes the sibling comparison through omega variables and cs_structure.reading_relations.

omegas.question: Is the formal contract/supervision test, as currently applied to platform work, still tracking a genuine independent-contracting relationship, or has it been engineered around by platform operators to avoid a substantively employment-like relationship?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Comparative analysis of the degree of algorithmic control (route assignment, pricing, deactivation authority, rating-linked discipline) exercised over platform workers versus the degree of control exercised in cases historically found to be genuine independent contracting; court findings in ongoing and resolved misclassification litigation across multiple jurisdictions.
omegas.impact: If the test is being engineered around, the formalist reading authored here is a constructed cover for cost externalization rather than a genuine boundary detection, and the substantive_employment_reading would be the structurally accurate account of the same population. If the test still tracks genuine independence for the median platform worker, the formalist reading holds and the extraction measured here reflects a legitimate cost structure rather than externalization.
omegas.description: Whether the formal test is genuinely tracking independence or has been engineered around.

omegas.question: What share of the platform workforce is genuinely the flexibility-seeking minority (for whom the formalist reading's exclusion from employment protection is a benefit, not a harm) versus the primary-income-dependent majority (for whom exclusion is a cost externalization)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Worker survey data disaggregating platform income as primary versus supplementary, cross-referenced with stated preference for employment status versus contractor flexibility, ideally longitudinal to separate stated preference from adaptive preference formed under lack of alternatives.
omegas.impact: A workforce composition skewed toward primary-income dependence would substantially undercut the formalist reading's beneficiary claim for the flexibility-seeking cohort and support a higher-victim-count reading; a workforce genuinely dominated by flexibility-seekers would support treating the formalist reading's beneficiary set as broader than authored here.
omegas.description: Composition of the platform workforce by dependence on gig income as primary versus supplementary.

omegas.question: This constraint is one reading of the employment_boundary kernel; the disagreement with substantive_employment_reading is located specifically in whether algorithmic control constitutes 'supervision' for legal purposes. Is that a factual question about the nature of algorithmic management, or an irreducibly normative choice about how broadly to define supervision?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Technical audit of algorithmic management systems to characterize the degree of real-time behavioral control exercised, combined with comparative legal analysis of how 'supervision' has been defined and expanded historically (e.g., the shift from direct foreman oversight to standardized-procedure supervision in manufacturing).
omegas.impact: If algorithmic control is factually equivalent in kind to direct supervision (just executed by software rather than a human foreman), the formalist reading's premise — that no supervision exists — becomes empirically false rather than merely contested, which would sharply narrow this reading's defensible scope. If the equivalence is genuinely a normative extension rather than a factual finding, the formalist and substantive readings remain a live values disagreement rather than one being simply mistaken.
omegas.description: Whether the formalist/substantive disagreement over algorithmic control is empirical or normative in character.

network.dual_formulation_note: This story is one of three linked constraints decomposing the natural-language concept 'employment boundary' per the ε-invariance principle. formalist_employment_reading (this story) authors ε=0.78 with platforms/investors as beneficiaries and workers/public insurers/competing employers as victims. substantive_employment_reading authors a structurally different constraint with a broader victim set (the full-time gig workforce reclassified as misclassified employees) and would show different or higher ε depending on how thoroughly cost externalization is measured under that reading's own terms. hybrid_security_reading rejects the binary entirely and would author a coordination-dominant profile without a symmetric beneficiary/victim split, since its founding premise is that neither existing category fits. All three share the kernel_id employment_boundary and are linked bidirectionally via affects_constraints; none averages or blends the others' ε.
